questions.prompt: You run adfuller on a gap between two prices and get a p-value of 0.003. What does that tell you?
options: The gap is a random walk
The test cannot tell the gap from a random walk
The gap will close within 3 days
The test rejects the random walk, so the gap looks stationary
questions.explanation: The ADF test starts from 'this is a random walk'. A p-value below 0.05 rejects that, which is evidence the gap is pulled back to its mean.

questions.prompt: A price series gives an ADF p-value of 0.83. Which reading is correct?
options: The price is proven to be a random walk
There is no evidence of a pull back to a level, so mean reversion on this price has no support from the test
The price is stationary with 83% confidence
The price returns to its mean 83% of the time
questions.explanation: A large p-value means the test cannot tell the series from a random walk. It is not proof of a random walk, but it gives no evidence of a pull either.

questions.prompt: In the example, the walk's mean was -20.95 in the first 250 days and -43.35 in the next 250. Why does that matter?
options: A stationary series keeps the same mean over time, so a moving mean is a sign of a random walk
It shows the walk has a stronger pull than the other series
It means the random steps were larger in the second half
It shows the ADF test was run on too few days
questions.explanation: A random walk has no level to return to, so its average drifts from one period to the next. The pulled series stayed near 0 in both halves.
